messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 73
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Journalist
  trauma_type: Man-made disaster
  pcl5: 74

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Visual (Photos): Related photos, Unpredictability: Unpredictable situations, Gustatory (Taste): A specific taste associated with the event
  Maladaptive Strategies: Sit With Back to Wall: always sit with back against a wall to see the room, Compulsive Spending: I spend money impulsively to distract or comfort myself, Freeze When Threatened: freeze completely when feeling threatened
  Threat: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Noticing Weapons: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment
  Memory: Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me, Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over., Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.
  Negative Appraisals: Thought Avoidance: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it, Lost Emotions: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again, Lost Meaning: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

George was seventy-three years old, a retired journalist who had spent decades covering urban conflict, but nothing had prepared him for the morning of the City Market bombing. He had arrived early to photograph the crowd for a human-interest piece. The detonation came from a parked delivery van—a man-made disaster, he would later learn, orchestrated by a fringe group. In the seconds after the blast, George saw limbs and debris rising, tasted the thick, metallic tang of blood and the acrid burn of explosives settling on his tongue. He helped drag survivors from the rubble until emergency crews arrived, then filed his report, including the photos he had taken. In the weeks that followed, he tried to move on, but the memory refused to fade. The taste—sharp, coppery, chemical—returned unexpectedly when he bit into certain foods, and he began avoiding anything that might trigger that sensory echo. His own photographs, published widely in newspapers, became unbearable; he could no longer look at images of crowds or even news coverage of other disasters without feeling the ground shift beneath him.

At first, George told himself the reaction was normal, that he would settle back into routine. But he started to notice small changes in how he moved through the world. In his apartment, he sat only with his back against a wall, positioned so he could see every doorway. He began listening—really listening—for sounds that might mean someone was entering his home: the creak of a floorboard, the faint turn of a lock. In public, his eyes scanned tables for knives, for glass bottles, for anything that could become a weapon. Unpredictable situations—a car backfiring, a sudden shout—made him freeze completely, stuck in place until his heart slowed. He became certain that if he let himself think about the bombing in any detail, he would fall apart, so he pushed the thoughts down, tried to keep his mind busy. That was when the spending started: he bought expensive camera equipment he did not need, then furniture, then clothes, charging thousands of dollars to his credit card in a kind of urgent, hollow rush that temporarily drowned out the replays in his head. The replays were the worst—a film that looped without permission, showing the same bodies, the same smoke, the same faces, until he felt as though it was happening right then, in his living room, his body braced for impact. And yet, when the feeling passed, the memories seemed unreal, too extreme to have happened to him; sometimes he wondered if he had imagined the whole thing.

Over the months and years, George became a ghost in his own life. His divorce, years before the event, had already left him isolated, but now he found it impossible to connect with his adult daughter or his few remaining friends. He had lost the capacity for normal emotions, he believed—nothing felt genuine anymore, and when he tried to laugh or care, the sensation was flat, distant. He retired early, not because he needed to but because nothing in his work felt meaningful. The stories he had spent a lifetime chasing now seemed empty, and he questioned what he had ever been trying to accomplish. He stopped answering phone calls. He stopped going to restaurants because the unpredictability of the environment was too much—people walking behind him, sudden noises from the kitchen—and even his own home no longer felt safe, because he could not relax anywhere, not even when he locked the doors.

What finally brought George to seek help was his daughter, who visited after a long silence and found him sitting in the dark, his back to the wall, staring at nothing. She told him she was frightened for him. He agreed to see a therapist, not because he believed it would work, but because he could no longer stand the numbness. He told the clinician he wanted to feel something real again, even if that meant facing the memories he had worked so hard to avoid. But what he feared most was that the moment he started to let the memories in, they would swallow him whole, and he would never find his way back.
